beats.narration: Begin by framing Robot Software Architecture Overview as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Robot software separates sensing, state estimation, planning, control, and actuation while making message contracts and timing assumptions explicit. Consider this worked case: A navigation stack uses a perception node to publish camera data, a localization node to estimate pose, a planner to generate waypoints, a controller to compute velocities, and an actuator driver to send commands to wheels. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Robot Software Architecture Overview
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a layered block diagram showing five stacked modules (sensing, state estimation, planning, control, actuation) with bidirectional arrows indicating data flow and explicit timing labels on each interface.

beats.narration: Now define ROS 2 Node Communication Model precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. ROS 2 organizes a robot application as nodes that communicate through typed interfaces. Consider this worked case: A localization node subscribes to a topic publishing IMU data, while a planning service handles a request-response call to compute a path between two waypoints. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: ROS 2 Node Communication Model
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a network diagram with labeled nodes connected by color-coded lines representing topics (dashed), services (solid), and actions (dotted), with message type tags on each line.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Parameter Configuration and Behavior operates in a concrete sequence. Parameters configure node behavior. Consider this worked case: A controller node uses a parameter named 'max_speed' to cap wheel velocity, which can be updated via a ROS 2 parameter server during simulation. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Parameter Configuration and Behavior
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a configuration panel with key-value pairs for robot parameters, highlighting how changing a single value propagates to the corresponding node's behavior settings.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Coordinate Transforms and Reference Frames and make the decision criteria explicit. Coordinate transforms describe relationships among reference frames. Consider this worked case: A camera's local image coordinates are transformed into the robot's base link frame using a rotation matrix and translation vector to align with the map. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Coordinate Transforms and Reference Frames
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate two overlapping coordinate grids (local and global) with labeled axes, showing a transformation arrow and matrix notation connecting them.

beats.narration: Apply Sensor Timestamping and Frame Interpretation to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Sensors produce observations that must be timestamped and interpreted in the correct frame. Consider this worked case: LiDAR scans are tagged with a precise timestamp and attached to the robot's odometry frame, ensuring they align temporally with camera and IMU data. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Sensor Timestamping and Frame Interpretation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a timeline with synchronized sensor events, each marked with a timestamp and frame label, connected to a central synchronization node.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Reactive Motion Control Principles, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Consider this worked case: A velocity controller reduces forward speed when a proximity sensor detects an obstacle within two meters, preventing collisions without full replanning. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Reactive Motion Control Principles
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-view simulation of a robot approaching a wall, with a reactive control loop highlighted, displaying input sensor data, computed velocity, and output wheel commands.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Map Building and Localization with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Consider this worked case: A SLAM algorithm fuses wheel odometry and camera images to update a grid map, then uses feature matching to locate the robot's current pose. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Map Building and Localization
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a top-down map grid with a moving robot icon, showing how sensor observations incrementally fill in map cells and update the robot's position marker.

beats.narration: Use Path Planning in Dynamic Environments to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Consider this worked case: A reactive planner recalculates a route when a moving pedestrian enters the robot's path, inserting a detour that maintains safety margins and task completion time. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Path Planning in Dynamic Environments
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a navigation map with a planned path, a dynamic obstacle, and a revised path, using color coding to distinguish static obstacles, dynamic hazards, and planned trajectories.

beats.narration: Connect Simulation and Physical Deployment to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Testing should consider latency, dropped messages, sensor noise, actuator limits, safety boundaries, and the difference between simulation and physical operation. Consider this worked case: A navigation algorithm is first validated in a physics engine simulation, then deployed on a wheeled robot to verify real-world performance and adjust parameters accordingly. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Simulation and Physical Deployment
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a split-screen comparison: left side shows a simulation environment with debug overlays, right side shows a physical robot with sensor data feeds and control interfaces.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, thresholds, coordinate frames, and evaluation metrics. Consider this worked case: A developer checks that message latency stays below 50 milliseconds, verifies sensor noise does not exceed calibration thresholds, and confirms safety zones are enforced before field testing. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a checklist graphic with five categories (latency, message integrity, sensor noise, actuator limits, safety boundaries), each with a pass/fail indicator and a brief validation method.

sources.author: OpenCV
sources.excerpt: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, thresholds, coordinate frames, and evaluation metrics.
